newsitem.title: MEXICO: INSTANT VIEW - Mexico Q3 GDP seen boosting markets.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Mexico Q3 GDP seen boosting markets.

text.p: A 7.4 percent year-on-year rise in third quarter Mexican gross domestic product shows a stronger-than-expected recovery that should cheer the gloomy equity market, economists said on Thursday.
"The markets are going to take it very well. We were thinking it would be a good recovery, but not this good," said Carlos Rosales, an economist at Bancomer.

In a Reuters survey, analysts had expected a rise of 6.47 percent in Q3 GDP, though shortly prior to the data's release, some bumped up their forecasts because of a surge in September industrial activity reported on Monday.
Rosales said his bank had taken into account the industrial output data, but had been sceptical about the strength of the services sector that comprises about three-quarters of GDP.
"It's incredible," he said of the 5.4 percent increase in the services sector, which was well above Bancomer's four percent projected rise.

He said signs of activity in the services sector, reflecting a slowly recovering domestic economy, tallied with a sharp rise in consumer goods imports reported in an October preliminary trade report issued late Wednesday. It suggested the fourth quarter would remain robust.

"Growth continues to be very strong," said Enrique Ramirez, economist at Santander that had recently bumped up its forecast to a spot-on 7.4 percent because of the thriving industrial sector. "Hardly anyone thought after the Q2 (7.2 percent) GDP rise that it would be higher in the third quarter."

He noted that the 5.4 percent services increase was the same as in Q2. He said it showed domestic consumption was staging an "important recovery," even though it was not as strong as the export-led industrial sector.
On the equities side, analysts said the surprisingly narrow $277 million October trade surplus was also positive.
Hector Velez of Inverlat, whose forecast was close to the actual number, said seasonal factors narrowed the surplus, but he expected a positive balance to hold for the rest of 1996.
But another economist, who asked not to be identified, warned that a 50.5 percent surge in consumer imports augured poorly for the future.

"The surplus is running out. We're closer to seeing monthly deficits," he said. "That is going to be viewed more negatively than positively. It's going to encourage exporters to press for a weaker peso, a line the foreigners will take tOo because it's in their interests."
